text:
British Airways, Delta, and American Airlines are not just giants in the sky—they are the driving force behind the most significant tourism boom the world has seen since the pandemic. With global travel demand soaring to unprecedented heights in 2026, these airlines have expanded their flight networks, bringing travelers from the United States to the United Kingdom, France, and beyond, connecting them with some of the world’s most coveted destinations. From New York to London, and Paris to Los Angeles, these aviation leaders are shaping the future of tourism, fueling a resurgence that is leaving a profound impact on both the airline and hospitality industries. Hotels and resorts in these key markets are experiencing record-breaking occupancy rates, exceeding pre-pandemic levels, as tourists flock to vibrant cities for business, leisure, and cultural exploration. With British Airways doubling down on its long-haul routes and Delta and American Airlines offering more direct flights, the travel experience has become more seamless than ever. As flights fill up and hotel rooms become a rare commodity, the dynamic relationship between these airlines and the hospitality sector is creating a perfect storm of opportunity for both industries. Travelers are not just booking flights—they are securing seats on the first wave of a global tourism renaissance, ready to explore a world that has, at last, reopened its doors.

British Airways, Delta & American Airlines Drive Tourism Surge in UK, USA, and France — Hotels, Resorts, and Airlines Smash Pre‑COVID Travel Records

The global travel industry is experiencing a historic surge in tourism, driven by key players like British Airways, Delta Air Lines, and American Airlines, as they revitalize transatlantic travel. The significant expansion of these airlines’ services is reshaping international tourism, particularly in popular destinations such as the UK, USA, and France. As travel demand accelerates, hotels and resorts in these regions are witnessing record-breaking bookings, surpassing pre-pandemic levels. This growth has created an interconnected boom between the airline and hospitality industries, driving both higher flight capacities and elevated hotel revenues.

This article takes a closer look at how British Airways and its counterparts are reshaping global tourism by bolstering flight offerings to major destinations and boosting the hospitality sector with sustained growth. We’ll also explore travel-friendly tips, flight details, and expert recommendations for tourists planning their next getaway.

British Airways, Delta, and American Airlines Power Growth in Global Tourism

In 2026, the global travel market has witnessed a significant rebound, with British Airways, Delta, and American Airlines leading the way by expanding their flight networks and increasing service frequencies across key international routes. These airlines have strategically enhanced their offerings, focusing on high-demand destinations such as the United Kingdom, United States, and France.

As tourism demand skyrockets, airlines are investing in fleet upgrades and modern aircraft such as the Airbus A350 and Boeing 787. British Airways alone has introduced additional flights from London Heathrow to New York and Los Angeles, providing seamless connections for business and leisure travelers alike. Delta and American Airlines have followed suit by offering more direct flights from cities like Chicago and Miami to London and Paris, strengthening connectivity and enabling travelers to enjoy a stress-free journey.

For tourists, these expanded services make it easier to reach some of the most popular destinations in the world, whether for sightseeing, business, or cultural exploration. This uptick in connectivity supports the ongoing recovery of global tourism, positioning these airlines at the forefront of travel excellence.

Hotels, Resorts, and Airlines Smash Pre‑COVID Travel Records in the UK, USA, and France

As the demand for international flights skyrockets, so does the need for accommodations. Hotels and resorts in the United Kingdom, United States, and France are seeing occupancy rates that surpass those of pre-pandemic levels, driven by both returning travelers and new visitors from across the globe. These regions, long-time favorites for international tourism, are benefiting immensely from the airline industry’s rebound.

In the United Kingdom, major cities such as London, Edinburgh, and Manchester are experiencing heightened demand for hotel rooms, especially among business travelers, international tourists, and families. London’s iconic landmarks, from Buckingham Palace to the British Museum, continue to attract millions, with a strong influx of visitors from North America. The strategic expansion of British Airways flights to New York and other key cities has directly influenced this growth, with Hyatt, Marriott, and Hilton hotels reporting a sharp increase in bookings.

Similarly, in the USA, cities like New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago are bustling with tourists eager to experience the American dream. The growth of Delta’s and American Airlines’ flight offerings to these key cities has allowed for easier access to these vibrant urban centers. Hotels such as The Langham in New York and The Four Seasons in Los Angeles are seeing full occupancy rates throughout the year. With global flight connections, especially from European and Asian markets, travelers can now enjoy a seamless travel experience from airport to hotel, enjoying the finest hospitality in the world.

France, renowned for its cultural heritage, world-class cuisine, and romance, is also thriving. Paris remains the most visited city in the world, with major hotel chains and boutique properties enjoying full occupancy rates as travelers return. The Champs-Élysées, Eiffel Tower, and Louvre Museum continue to allure millions of visitors, fueled by increased American and British flights landing daily at Charles de Gaulle airport. Hotels in Paris, such as The Ritz Paris and Le Meurice, are enjoying high-end bookings from luxury travelers, while mid-range chains like Ibis are experiencing steady demand as tourists flock to explore the French capital’s picturesque streets.

For tourists, this represents a fantastic opportunity to experience some of the world’s most coveted destinations. With increased availability of flights and diverse accommodation options, the once-limited availability of rooms during peak seasons is now becoming a thing of the past.

The Effect of Increased Airline Offerings on Tourist Choices

The surge in available flights from British Airways, Delta, and American Airlines has not only made international travel more accessible but has also reshaped tourist choices. In the USA, UK, and France, travelers now have more flexibility when choosing dates, times, and routes, allowing for a customized travel experience.

For instance, British Airways has introduced new routes from London Heathrow to Los Angeles, Miami, and Chicago, offering travelers more choices when planning their vacations or business trips. Similarly, American Airlines has expanded its direct flights to Paris and London, making these destinations more accessible to North American tourists. Delta Air Lines has also been proactive, launching flights to European cities, thereby increasing the pool of options for vacationers from the United States and other parts of the world.

With these options available, travelers are no longer confined to a single flight time or limited routes. The ability to choose flexible flight schedules increases customer satisfaction and enhances the overall travel experience, making these airlines the go-to choice for many tourists.

Expanding Airline Networks: A Boost for Hospitality and Travel Services

As the number of inbound and outbound flights increases, it is clear that airlines are no longer simply transportation services — they are becoming central to the entire travel ecosystem. British Airways, Delta, and American Airlines provide connections not only to major cities but also to secondary markets. This expansion drives higher occupancy rates for hotels in smaller cities as tourists look beyond traditional destinations. The American and European airlines’ increased focus on regional U.S. markets like Seattle and Austin has opened new opportunities for visitors to experience destinations that were previously less accessible. For travelers, this means more options for off-the-beaten-path explorations, including boutique hotels and charming local guesthouses.

Additionally, the hospitality industry is thriving thanks to these airlines’ promotions of unique travel packages. By partnering with Marriott, Hilton, and Hyatt, these airlines are offering special deals that combine airfares and hotel stays into discounted travel packages, designed to give tourists better value for their money.

Travelers’ Action Checklist

Book Early for Best Flight Options – With the surge in tourism, flights to New York, London, and Paris are filling up quickly. Plan ahead and book your tickets early to secure the best prices and seating options.

Use Airline–Hotel Packages – Many airlines are offering travel packages that include flights and hotel stays, which can save you money and time. Check for deals on British Airways, Delta, and American Airlines websites.

Choose Flexible Dates – Traveling during off-peak times can save you money. Explore flexible dates to avoid the busiest travel periods.

Consider Regional Travel – While London, Paris, and New York are popular tourist hubs, consider visiting secondary cities like Manchester, Chicago, or Seville, which are gaining popularity due to increased flight availability.

Research Hotel Options – Whether you prefer luxury hotels or budget-friendly accommodations, make sure to book in advance. Look for special offers on Hyatt, Marriott, and Hilton websites.

Check COVID-19 Travel Regulations – Ensure you are up-to-date with any entry requirements, such as vaccinations or testing protocols, for international travel.

Travel Light and Smart – Take advantage of the increased number of direct flights to avoid layovers. Pack light to make the most of your journey and enjoy the added convenience of faster travel.

The Future of Travel: Post-Pandemic Rebound and Sustainability Focus

Looking ahead, the post-pandemic recovery shows no signs of slowing down. Airlines like British Airways, Delta, and American Airlines continue to enhance their services to accommodate the ever-growing demand. Sustainability remains a key focus for the industry, with many airlines pledging to adopt green aviation technologies, including sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and carbon offset programs. This is not only reducing the environmental impact of air travel but also appealing to eco-conscious tourists.

The tourism sector will continue to thrive as the airline industry strengthens its position. The integration of flights and hotels, along with the expansion of travel networks, will ensure that 2026 sees another year of record-breaking travel across the globe.

title: Cebu Pacific Secures Jet Fuel Amid Global Supply Shock - The Traveler
description:
Cebu Pacific has secured sufficient jet fuel supplies to keep its flight schedule running even as a widening global energy crisis disrupts fuel markets, alarms travelers, and forces airlines worldwide to slash capacity.
In this high-pressure context, Cebu Pacific’s ability to publicly signal continuity of operations stands out.
Network Adjustments but Core Operations Remain Intact Despite securing jet fuel, Cebu Pacific has not been completely insulated from the upheaval in global energy markets.
Regional Carriers Scramble as Jet Fuel Costs Soar The contrast with other carriers across Asia and beyond helps explain why Cebu Pacific’s fuel security has gained such attention in travel circles.
What Cebu Pacific’s Fuel Hedge Means for Travelers For travelers in and out of the Philippines, Cebu Pacific’s secured jet fuel supplies offer a measure of predictability amid mounting uncertainty.
text:
Cebu Pacific has secured sufficient jet fuel supplies to keep its flight schedule running even as a widening global energy crisis disrupts fuel markets, alarms travelers, and forces airlines worldwide to slash capacity.

Image by Travel And Tour World

Strategic Fuel Deals Defy Mounting Global Shortages

Cebu Pacific’s fuel position emerges against a backdrop of unprecedented volatility in global oil markets triggered by the war in Iran and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for crude and refined products. Industry analysis shows that jet fuel prices in key trading hubs such as Singapore have more than doubled compared with 2025 averages, with traders reporting record premiums over crude and signs of physical shortages rather than just speculative spikes.

Publicly available information on aviation fuel markets indicates that refineries in Asia are cutting runs as supply chains strain under disrupted tanker traffic, while governments across the region scramble to secure alternative cargoes. In this context, securing a predictable stream of jet fuel has become one of the most serious operational risks for airlines, particularly for carriers in import-dependent countries like the Philippines.

While Cebu Pacific has not publicly detailed the full terms of its jet fuel arrangements, reports circulating in Philippine aviation circles and traveler forums indicate that the airline has locked in enough supply to cover its near-term schedule, with some sources suggesting coverage extending at least until June 2026. Market observers note that this compares favorably with the wider Philippine fuel market, where major oil firms have stated that national inventories are only firmly guaranteed through May.

Aviation analysts point to Cebu Pacific’s earlier strategy of shifting to more fuel-efficient Airbus A320neo-family aircraft and entering medium-term supply agreements, including sustainable aviation fuel offtake, as factors that may now be cushioning the carrier. These steps, originally framed as cost and emissions measures, have unexpectedly become critical hedges against the current price and supply shock.

Philippines Faces National Energy Emergency as Airlines Struggle

The airline’s apparent success in securing jet fuel contrasts sharply with the wider energy picture in the Philippines. The country declared a national energy emergency in late March after the government and industry groups warned that oil stockpiles were falling rapidly and replacement cargoes were increasingly hard to source. Economic reports describe the crisis as the most severe energy security challenge in decades, with the Philippines among the Asian economies most exposed to Gulf supply risks.

Domestic motorists and businesses are already feeling the strain. Local coverage describes diesel prices more than doubling from 2025 levels, triggering street protests by public transport operators and prompting the government to temporarily authorize the use of cheaper, lower-standard Euro II fuels. Officials have also rolled out work-week adjustments and other conservation measures in an effort to curb consumption and stretch limited inventories.

Aviation has been hit particularly hard. Airlines operating in and out of the Philippines have begun cutting frequencies, consolidating services, and introducing steep fuel surcharges on tickets sold for April and beyond. Regional carriers from Korea to Southeast Asia are similarly trimming networks or warning of further reductions, citing jet fuel costs that now represent an even larger share of operating expenses.

In this high-pressure context, Cebu Pacific’s ability to publicly signal continuity of operations stands out. Travelers comparing advisories from different airlines are finding a widening gap between carriers that can guarantee fuel availability for the coming months and those that are signaling that further cancellations or schedule thinning are possible if the crisis persists.

Network Adjustments but Core Operations Remain Intact

Despite securing jet fuel, Cebu Pacific has not been completely insulated from the upheaval in global energy markets. The airline has announced temporary network adjustments in response to the Middle East crisis, including selective frequency reductions and targeted flight cancellations. Public travel advisories emphasize that these changes are framed as capacity optimization and fuel conservation measures designed to preserve the integrity of the broader network.

Available advisories indicate that the carrier is prioritizing core domestic routes and key regional links while trimming less time-sensitive or lower-demand services. Aviation watchers note that this mirrors strategies adopted by other airlines worldwide, which are reallocating scarce fuel and aircraft capacity toward routes that are strategically or financially critical.

For passengers, the picture is mixed. Many Cebu Pacific customers report that their flights remain unaffected, particularly on major trunk routes, while others have received notifications of schedule changes or consolidations. Industry commentators say this reflects a deliberate balancing act: using the breathing room provided by secured fuel contracts to avoid mass cancellations, while still preemptively cutting some services to build resilience if the crisis deepens.

The airline’s current stance positions it somewhere between full crisis mode and business as usual. By confirming that it has sufficient jet fuel for the months ahead, Cebu Pacific is sending a signal of relative stability to travelers and tourism stakeholders, even as it prepares for what could be a protracted period of elevated prices and intermittent supply strains.

Regional Carriers Scramble as Jet Fuel Costs Soar

Reports from financial and aviation outlets show low-cost and full-service airlines from North America to Europe and East Asia revising earnings guidance, introducing new rounds of surcharges, and in some cases pulling capacity from marginal routes as jet fuel prices soar.

In Asia, where a significant share of jet fuel exports normally transits through the Gulf, analysts highlight the particular vulnerability of low-cost carriers reliant on high aircraft utilization and thin margins. Some Korean and regional Southeast Asian budget airlines have already announced route suspensions and capacity cuts, citing both the spike in fuel costs and currency pressures as reasons for retrenchment.

Global commentary on the crisis increasingly frames it as a structural test of airline resilience rather than a short-lived price shock. Carriers that locked in supply earlier, invested in more efficient fleets, or diversified their fuel sources appear better placed to navigate the current turmoil. Cebu Pacific’s recent fleet modernization drives and fuel arrangements, initially seen as incremental improvements, now appear to have given the airline an operational buffer that many rivals lack.

Travel industry analysts warn, however, that no carrier is fully insulated if the conflict in the Middle East and resulting disruptions to maritime energy flows persist for many more months. Even airlines with current coverage may face sharply higher renewal costs or reduced volumes once existing contracts roll off, potentially leading to a second wave of network changes later in the year.

For travelers in and out of the Philippines, Cebu Pacific’s secured jet fuel supplies offer a measure of predictability amid mounting uncertainty. While fares are already rising as fuel surcharges are adjusted upward across the industry, the airline’s ability to maintain a broad schedule reduces the immediate risk of widespread flight disruptions for summer and early autumn trips.

Tourism operators, hotels, and local governments in popular Philippine destinations are watching the situation closely. The country’s designation of a national energy emergency, combined with tighter household and business budgets due to higher fuel and electricity costs, has raised concerns about a slowdown in domestic travel. Cebu Pacific’s position, along with similar moves by other major carriers serving the archipelago, will be a key factor in determining how strongly the tourism sector weathers the crisis.

Travel planners note that passengers should still build extra flexibility into itineraries, as selective schedule changes remain possible and airport operations may be affected by broader energy-saving measures. Nonetheless, the current indicators suggest that Cebu Pacific, bolstered by its fuel arrangements and fleet strategy, is better prepared than many to keep its network aloft as the global fuel crisis continues to evolve.

In a year already marked by record jet fuel prices, shipping disruptions, and intensifying competition for limited supplies, Cebu Pacific’s fuel security stands as a rare piece of relatively positive news for travelers watching the world’s energy maps redraw in real time.

text:
The UK aviation sector is turning to pilot behaviour as a new front in the drive to cut fuel consumption and carbon emissions, with British Airways highlighting training and performance monitoring and fresh debate emerging over the use of incentives to encourage more efficient flying.

Image by Travel and Tour World – Tourism, Airline, Destination, MICE, Gobal Travel Market, Hotel news that you will find only over here.

Aviation Policy Puts Efficiency in the Climate Spotlight

The UK’s aviation decarbonisation agenda is increasingly focused on squeezing more efficiency out of existing aircraft while longer term technologies such as hydrogen propulsion and large-scale sustainable aviation fuel production mature. Government strategies and the UK Civil Aviation Authority’s climate work emphasise operational improvements alongside cleaner fuels and new aircraft designs as part of the path to net zero by 2050.

Publicly available information on UK policy notes that aviation operators are expected to pursue efficiency gains across the whole system, including through more efficient fleets and better day-to-day operations. Within that package, pilot decision making is seen as a key lever because it directly affects fuel load, speed management, routing and taxi procedures, all of which influence fuel burn on every flight.

At the same time, UK-backed research programmes are examining how operational choices contribute not only to carbon dioxide emissions but also to non-CO2 impacts such as contrails. Trials involving alternative fuels and different flight profiles aim to understand how pilots can reduce the formation of persistent contrails, which scientists link to additional warming.

The growing policy interest in operational behaviour is now intersecting with airline-level initiatives that seek to align individual pilot actions with corporate emissions targets, sharpening the focus on whether and how financial incentives should be used.

British Airways Leans on Training and Data to Change Pilot Habits

British Airways, part of International Airlines Group, has described pilot behaviour as central to its fuel-efficiency and emissions strategy. Public sustainability disclosures indicate that the carrier has integrated environmental topics into pilot training and simulator checks, with modules dedicated to areas such as reduced-engine taxiing and smarter use of discretionary fuel.

Recent sustainability reporting from the airline states that more than 4,000 pilots, representing the vast majority of its flight crew, have completed an annual flight sustainability training programme. That training focuses on techniques that are already permitted within existing safety margins, including optimising taxi procedures, fine-tuning climb and cruise settings, and avoiding unnecessary extra fuel uplift when conditions allow.

British Airways pairs this training with detailed flight data analysis. Operational information from each sector is used to monitor how often recommended fuel-saving techniques are applied. The airline presents this as a “pilot-first” approach, where captains receive feedback on their personal contribution to fuel efficiency and emissions rather than only seeing fleet-wide averages.

The company positions these efforts alongside wider decarbonisation measures such as renewing its fleet with more efficient aircraft, investing in sustainable aviation fuel and purchasing carbon removal credits. However, the specific question of financial incentives for pilots has become more prominent as the industry looks for low-cost ways to drive behavioural change.

Behavioural Science Inspires Incentive-Based Approaches

Interest in pilot incentives has been shaped by earlier behavioural-science trials in the UK, including a well-known study conducted with Virgin Atlantic a decade ago. That randomised experiment tested the impact of giving pilots personalised performance feedback, allowing them to set fuel-saving goals and, in some treatment groups, offering charitable donations when goals were achieved.

Research findings from that project reported that low-cost interventions could deliver significant fuel savings and emissions reductions without altering flight safety rules or onboard service. The study indicated that simply reporting performance back to pilots and enabling goal-setting led to measurable improvements, while the addition of non-cash rewards strengthened the effect.

Although that trial involved a different UK airline, it has influenced thinking across the sector, including at British Airways, about the potential for incentive-style schemes to support efficiency programmes. Behavioural insights specialists argue that pilots, like other professionals, respond to clear goals, timely feedback and meaningful rewards, and that these tools can complement traditional training and procedures.

In practice, modern programmes typically combine advanced data analytics with behavioural techniques. Airlines can now track adherence to fuel-saving procedures in near real time and present tailored dashboards to individual pilots and fleets, raising the possibility of linking performance metrics to recognition schemes, bonuses or other incentives.

Safety Concerns and Regulatory Scrutiny Around Fuel Bonuses

The idea of directly linking pilots’ pay or bonuses to fuel savings has, however, prompted strong debate. Recent online discussions referencing British Airways and other carriers highlight concerns that poorly designed incentive schemes could encourage pilots to take less fuel than they might otherwise choose, potentially narrowing safety margins in abnormal or rapidly changing conditions.

Critics argue that any financial reward tied explicitly to fuel quantities risks creating a perceived conflict between cost savings and the conservative fuel-planning philosophy that underpins commercial aviation safety. Airline pilots commenting publicly often stress that performance programmes must never penalise captains for carrying extra fuel when they judge it necessary for weather, traffic, diversion risks or other operational uncertainties.

Regulators in the UK and elsewhere have not issued blanket bans on incentives, but available guidance and industry commentary consistently emphasise that safety requirements and fuel reserve rules cannot be compromised. Schemes that focus on adherence to approved best practices, rather than absolute reductions in fuel uplift, are generally viewed as more acceptable.

As attention grows on incentive-based approaches, the UK Civil Aviation Authority’s broader work on aviation sustainability and safety oversight provides the framework within which any such programmes must operate. Industry observers expect regulators to continue scrutinising how airlines design and communicate incentives so that efficiency gains do not erode the longstanding safety culture.

Implications for Passengers and the UK’s Net Zero Path

For travellers, most of these changes are largely invisible. Fuel-efficiency initiatives driven by pilot behaviour typically play out behind the scenes, influencing how flights are planned and operated rather than altering the passenger experience in obvious ways. In some cases, passengers may notice small differences, such as shorter taxi times with one engine shut down or cruise profiles that feel slightly different from past journeys.

From a climate perspective, however, the cumulative impact of incremental savings across thousands of flights can be substantial. Studies of behaviour-focused trials suggest that operational changes can remove tens of thousands of tonnes of carbon dioxide at relatively low cost, making them an attractive complement to more capital-intensive measures such as new aircraft and fuel production facilities.

Within the UK’s wider Jet Zero ambition, pilot incentives and behaviour programmes are likely to remain one piece of a larger puzzle that includes sustainable aviation fuel mandates, hydrogen and electric aircraft development, renewable energy use at airports and market-based carbon measures. Efficiency gains achieved through cockpit decisions cannot on their own neutralise aviation’s climate footprint, but they can buy time and reduce emissions while longer-term technologies scale up.

As British Airways and other UK carriers refine their approaches, the balance between incentivising fuel savings and safeguarding conservative fuel planning will be closely watched. The outcome may shape not only corporate emissions trajectories but also public confidence in how airlines pursue efficiency in an era of heightened climate scrutiny.

By Mohamed Attia

Egypt’s Ministry of Civil Aviation, under the guidance of Minister of Civil Aviation Sameh Al-Hefny, has started using Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) to reduce carbon emissions by gradually phasing out fossil fuels, promote green investments, and ensure the sustainability of the aviation sector in line with the policies of the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO), Africa is also moving towards sustainability in aviation.

In a step reflecting the African continent’s move toward promoting sustainability in the aviation sector, a continental workshop on developing and deploying sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) policies, held in Pretoria, has concluded.

The workshop was held with high-level participation from policymakers, aviation experts, government representatives, and the private sector from various African countries. Egypt was represented by Captain Karim Gamal, Advisor to the Chairman of the Egyptian Civil Aviation Authority.

The workshop was held under the patronage of the African Union and the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa, as part of joint efforts to support the transition toward more sustainable aviation and to strengthen the continent’s ability to keep pace with global trends in reducing carbon emissions in the aviation sector.

The workshop included extensive discussions about the development mechanisms of the sustainable aviation fuel system in Africa, with the participants reviewing the strategic trends that aim to achieve energy security, open new economic prospects, and strengthen the local value chains in sectors related to energy and aviation.

The participants emphasised that the development of sustainable aviation fuel is a strategic opportunity for the African continent, as it offers significant potential to support economic growth and create new job opportunities, particularly in the aviation, petroleum, agriculture, industry, and transport sectors.

The discussions also stressed the importance of strengthening regional co-operation and continental integration through partnerships among African countries to pool resources and develop joint projects. This, in turn, will contribute to increasing investment in this vital sector.

The workshop, at its conclusion, recommended the need to introduce flexible and incentive policies for investment in sustainable aviation fuel, support innovation and scientific research, as well as strengthen public-private sector partnerships and work on developing unified regulatory frameworks at the continental level.

It is worth noting that this step comes at a time when the African aviation sector is witnessing rapid growth, making the transition to sustainable fuel an urgent necessity to ensure the sustainability of this growth and achieve the continent’s long-term development goals.

text:
North East Mayor Kim McGuinness says "we need to push the aviation industry" to improve its sustainability and reduce its carbon footprint. Climate campaigners accused Newcastle Airport of "smoke and mirrors" over its expansion plans, which it says will almost double passenger numbers to nine million per year by 2040 and generate £1.9 billion for the North East economy.

A number of environmental groups spoke to ChronicleLive, saying that the economic growth will not outweigh the environmental harm caused by running more flights. Speaking at the opening of easyJet's new base on Monday, Ms McGuinness said: "I think it's absolutely a fair challenge and we need to push the industry here to improve itself when it comes to sustainability and its carbon footprint."

However, she said that the airport's Masterplan showed a commitment to improving its environmental impact. She said: "It's good to see in that airport masterplan a commitment to things like more solar panels and sustainable aviation fuel.

READ MORE: {{title}}

"I would always encouraged them to do more and as quickly as possible, but at the same time we really want to see growth in our tourist industries here in the North East.

"We've got ambitious plans to double the number of tourists who visit us, stay overnight, everything we've got to offer in the region and give our brilliant hospitality sector a boost. This plan backs that, and so I'm really pleased about that, I think it's a positive thing."

Newcastle International Airport says it is on track to achieve net zero by 2035. However, it excludes emissions from flights taking off and landing from its net zero calculations and only includes factors over which it has "more direct control".

Leon McQuaid, director of aviation development at Newcastle Airport, said: "Naturally we're going to grow with jobs through the investment that comes with aviation but we want to ensure that we do that in a sustainable way. Scope one and two are the emissions that we can control as an airport, our airport on a sunny day is entirely run by our solar farm.

"We then look to how we offset scope three and four which would then include customers travelling to the airport and working with airlines on their carbon emissions."

title: Singapore Defers Green Jet Fuel Levy Amid Fuel Price Surge - The Traveler
description:
The delay does not cancel the sustainable aviation fuel policy framework.
Rising Jet Fuel Prices Reshape Cost Calculus The decision to defer the green levy is unfolding against a backdrop of significant volatility in global energy markets.
Against this backdrop, introducing an additional levy specifically earmarked for sustainable aviation fuel would have layered another cost on top of already elevated fuel expenses.
For travelers, the delay means that previously signalled increases linked specifically to sustainable aviation fuel will not appear on tickets in the coming weeks.
Singapore is also positioning itself as a potential regional hub for sustainable aviation fuel production, trading and certification.
text:
Singapore has delayed the introduction of a planned green jet fuel levy on departing air travelers, offering short term financial relief to airlines and passengers as jet fuel prices spike, while maintaining its long term commitment to sustainable aviation fuel and carbon reduction targets.

Image by Latest International / Global Travel News, Breaking World Travel News

Planned Sustainable Aviation Fuel Levy Put On Hold

Singapore had been preparing to introduce a green jet fuel levy tied to the use of sustainable aviation fuel on flights departing the city state, as part of a broader strategy to decarbonise aviation and position Changi Airport as a leading green hub in Asia. Publicly available policy documents and industry reports describe the levy as a key funding tool to close the price gap between conventional jet fuel and cleaner alternatives and to support national sustainable aviation fuel blending targets from the mid 2020s onward.

Reports in late March 2026 indicate that authorities have now deferred the rollout of the levy, which had been expected to start around April. The move comes at a time when airlines serving Singapore are already grappling with sharply higher fuel bills and surcharges linked to a surge in global oil and refined product prices following conflict in the Middle East and disruptions affecting shipping lanes.

The delay does not cancel the sustainable aviation fuel policy framework. Planning materials from aviation and transport agencies continue to refer to a phased ramp up of sustainable aviation fuel usage over the coming decade, with blending targets and a centralized procurement approach intended to give airlines certainty on supply and costs over the long term.

For now, however, the pause on the levy means that ticket prices for flights out of Singapore will not immediately reflect an additional green surcharge that had been widely anticipated by industry watchers and frequent flyers.

Rising Jet Fuel Prices Reshape Cost Calculus

The decision to defer the green levy is unfolding against a backdrop of significant volatility in global energy markets. Market commentary and economic analysis published in March 2026 highlight that bunker fuel and distillate products, including jet fuel, have risen steeply in price, reflecting higher crude benchmarks and supply constraints across key shipping and refining hubs.

Singapore, which is both a major refining center and an energy import dependent economy, is acutely exposed to these swings. Business and policy briefings note that in early 2026 some marine and aviation fuel grades sold in Singapore crossed price thresholds that would have been considered extreme only a few years earlier, increasing operating costs for airlines, shipping companies and logistics providers across the region.

Consumer oriented discussion in local media and online forums also points to higher pump prices for motorists and fuel related surcharges across different transport modes, from regional ferries to air tickets. Airlines serving Singapore have already adjusted base fares and fuel surcharges to partially offset the rise in operating costs, with travel industry analysts warning of further upward pressure on prices if energy markets remain tight.

Against this backdrop, introducing an additional levy specifically earmarked for sustainable aviation fuel would have layered another cost on top of already elevated fuel expenses. The deferral effectively slows the pace at which environmental charges are built into airfares at a time when households and businesses are still digesting broader energy related inflation.

Short Term Relief for Airlines and Travelers

For airlines, the postponement of the sustainable aviation fuel levy represents a modest but welcome reprieve for their cost bases in the near term. Network carriers and low cost operators alike face higher jet fuel bills, and while many use hedging strategies, the recent price spikes have still translated into thinner margins and pressure to raise fares on both regional and long haul routes.

Without the immediate addition of a green levy on tickets issued in Singapore, carriers have slightly more room to manage yields and promotional activity, particularly during shoulder seasons when demand is more price sensitive. Industry watchers expect some airlines to use this breathing space to preserve capacity and connectivity rather than pulling back routes or frequencies, which would have knock on effects for Singapore’s hub status.

For travelers, the delay means that previously signalled increases linked specifically to sustainable aviation fuel will not appear on tickets in the coming weeks. Passengers are still facing higher average fares compared with previous years, largely driven by fuel costs and strong post pandemic demand, but one additional line item in the final ticket price is, for the moment, off the table.

Travel agents and online booking platforms have been adjusting their fare calculators and consumer advisories in line with the evolving policy timeline. While there is no broad rollback in prices, the absence of a new levy in April bookings offers a degree of short term clarity for travelers planning trips through Singapore during peak school holiday and business travel periods.

Long Term Climate Goals and SAF Road Map Intact

Despite the near term deferral, Singapore’s long term decarbonisation plans for aviation remain firmly in place. Sustainability reports from the aviation sector and public policy statements continue to emphasize the central role of sustainable aviation fuel in meeting emissions reduction targets and preserving the competitiveness of Singapore as a global air hub.

Current frameworks outline a progressive approach in which sustainable aviation fuel blending is scaled up over time, supported by a combination of levies, incentives and centralized procurement to aggregate demand and reduce cost premiums. Airlines operating from Changi are expected to use a minimum share of sustainable aviation fuel in the coming years, rising toward higher percentages closer to 2030 and beyond as supply expands and technology matures.

Analysts note that the temporary postponement of the levy is better understood as a timing adjustment rather than a retreat from climate goals. The core policy logic remains that aviation must contribute to national and global decarbonisation efforts, and that pricing mechanisms that reflect carbon intensity will eventually be needed to align market behavior with those objectives.

Singapore is also positioning itself as a potential regional hub for sustainable aviation fuel production, trading and certification. Industry briefings and conference presentations highlight ongoing work to attract investment into feedstock supply chains, refining capacity and related infrastructure so that future sustainable aviation fuel demand can be met from diversified and resilient sources.

Balancing Affordability With the Cost of Transition

The delay of the green jet fuel levy underscores the policy tension between protecting consumers and businesses from sudden cost increases and sustaining momentum in the transition to low carbon aviation. Rising fuel prices due to geopolitical shocks have compressed the space in which new environmental charges can be introduced without triggering additional inflationary pressure.

Economic commentary focused on Singapore’s outlook for 2026 suggests that while overall growth is expected to remain positive, higher energy costs are already feeding into transportation, logistics and household expenses. In this environment, incremental policy steps that raise travel costs can carry outsized political and economic sensitivity, even when they serve long term environmental aims.

Observers expect Singapore to revisit the timing and structure of the sustainable aviation fuel levy once energy markets stabilize or when complementary measures are in place to cushion the impact on price sensitive travelers. Possible adjustments discussed in public debate include more differentiated levies by cabin class or distance, and targeted assistance for certain groups of travelers if needed.

For now, the postponement provides a window in which airlines, travelers and policymakers can reassess how best to share the costs of decarbonising aviation. As global attention turns to both climate commitments and energy security, Singapore’s handling of its green jet fuel levy is likely to be closely watched by other aviation hubs seeking to strike a similar balance between affordability and sustainability.

title: Op-Ed: In Indianapolis and Washington, D.C., 2026 Has Been a Busy Legislative Year
description:
With House Bill 1003, we saw the creation of the Agricultural Regulatory Task Force.
The House Agricultural Committee has voted its version of the 2026 Farm Bill out of committee.
One summer in college, I had the pleasure of working for the Senate Agriculture Committee.
That summer we spent a lot of time working on what would become the 1996 Farm Bill.
That bargain was broken last year, so we will have to see if this “skinny” farm bill will get across the finish line.
text:
INDIANAPOLIS — This year has proven to be busy, so far, when it comes to advocating for Indiana’s soybean farmers. At the Statehouse, we were successful in seeing the passage of Senate Bill 55 that provided a fallback state soybean checkoff in the event that the federal checkoff ceases to function. We are only waiting for Gov. Braun to sign it into law.

With House Bill 1003, we saw the creation of the Agricultural Regulatory Task Force. This task force will look at what changes need to be made to the structure of the Indiana State Department of Agriculture (ISDA). When the department was created, several agencies that align with agriculture were left out, such as the Indiana State Chemist and the Board of Animal Health.

This was because many wanted to see the ISDA act as a cheerleader and promoter of agriculture, not a regulator. This may be the time to re-evaluate that decision and consider what will make ISDA the best advocate for the state’s agricultural industry.

The Indiana Soybean Alliance will have a seat on that task force to represent you.

We have seen movement in Washington, D.C., as well, but we are a long way from the finish line.

The House Agricultural Committee has voted its version of the 2026 Farm Bill out of committee. From a soybean farmer’s perspective, there are several things to like about the House version – including increased reimbursement rates for precision agriculture in the Environmental Quality Incentives Program (EQIP). There is new funding in the Conservation Stewardship Program (CSP) for soil health initiatives.

The Energy Title helps lay out the groundwork for a strategy to grow demand and production capacity for sustainable aviation fuel. As this market takes off, it could be a huge win for soybean producers.

One summer in college, I had the pleasure of working for the Senate Agriculture Committee. That summer we spent a lot of time working on what would become the 1996 Farm Bill. I learned a lot that year. I learned the value of being engaged and advocating for your industry as I saw growers and lobbyists from every commodity walking the halls of Congress to push their messages.

I also learned about the “Grand Bargain,” the need to pair the titles important to most of us in production ag with the Nutrition title. For decades it was seen as critical to have this because it was argued that Ag alone wouldn’t have the votes in rural districts to get our bills across the finish line.

That bargain was broken last year, so we will have to see if this “skinny” farm bill will get across the finish line. It will be a challenge to get it done before the mid-term elections.

The Senate has yet to introduce their version of the farm bill. Sen. John Boozman (R-Ark.), chairman of the Senate Ag Committee, hasn’t laid out how his priorities will be different from the House’s version.

So, we will need to pay close attention to how the next steps in the process unfold and be ready to engage to make sure our voices are heard.

text:
SEMARANG, iNewsPurwokerto.id - PT Pertamina Patra Niaga Regional Jawa Bagian Tengah mencatat lonjakan konsumsi energi selama periode Satuan Tugas Ramadan dan Idulfitri (Satgas RAFI) 2026. Peningkatan ini sejalan dengan tingginya mobilitas masyarakat saat arus mudik dan arus balik Lebaran.

Berdasarkan data realisasi harian, konsumsi BBM ritel jenis gasoline mengalami kenaikan signifikan sebesar 28,4 persen, dari rata-rata normal 12.943 kiloliter (KL) menjadi 16.625 KL per hari. Sebaliknya, konsumsi gasoil justru turun 10,2 persen, dari 7.069 KL menjadi 6.350 KL per hari.

Lonjakan tertinggi gasoline terjadi pada 19 Maret 2026 dengan volume mencapai 20.681 KL, dipicu meningkatnya penggunaan kendaraan pribadi selama masa mudik.

Di sektor LPG, konsumsi juga menunjukkan tren peningkatan. Rata-rata harian LPG naik 6,7 persen dari 4.854 metrik ton (MT) menjadi 5.179 MT. Untuk LPG subsidi 3 kg, konsumsi meningkat 7,2 persen dari 4.630 MT menjadi 4.965 MT per hari. Sementara itu, LPG non-subsidi mengalami penurunan 4,7 persen dari 224 MT menjadi 214 MT per hari. Puncak konsumsi LPG tercatat pada 18 Maret 2026 dengan volume mencapai 5.424 MT.

Area Manager Communication, Relations, & CSR Regional Jawa Bagian Tengah, Taufiq Kurniawan, mengatakan Pertamina telah mengantisipasi lonjakan kebutuhan energi sejak awal Satgas RAFI, termasuk saat puncak arus balik.

“Secara regional, kami memastikan ketahanan energi tetap terjaga dengan ketersediaan stok mencapai 29,2 kali lipat dari rata-rata konsumsi harian,” ujarnya.

title: Why Do Airlines Keep Older Aircraft In Service Longer Than Expected? - Simple Flying
authors: Louis Hardiman, Aaron Bailey, Prachi Patel
description:

text:
Almost every carrier has some legacy jets in its fleet. Yet, these aren't just sitting around gathering dust, but play an important role in a carrier's operation, often carrying out missions that are not compatible with modern airliners. Common old narrowbody jets include outdated 737 and A320 variants, and the Boeing 757, the workhorse of United Airlines. Other notable aircraft that seem like they should be obsolete include the Airbus A380 and 747 superjumbos, and early A330s and 767s. Old jets are particularly popular among cargo carriers, who don't have to worry about passenger experience, and fly their aircraft less frequently.

Read on to learn more about why old aircraft continue to be mainstays for many of the world's best airlines, and which US carriers have the most prevalent old aircraft. The 717 is then used as a case study to investigate the unique capabilities of old aircraft.

Why We Expect Carriers Will Usually Prefer Newer Aircraft

To ask why carriers fly older aircraft than is expected, we first need to interrogate why we expect them to fly new aircraft. Passenger airliners love new aircraft because they come with fantastic cabin amenities and features that allow them to provide a more competitive passenger experience. For instance, the Boeing 787 Dreamliner comes with large windows, increased cabin pressure, and better air filtration systems. Passengers flying on such modern aircraft won't suffer so much from jet lag.

New aircraft like the Airbus A350 are also far more efficient. This allows the aviation industry to meet global sustainability goals as deadlines to reach net-zero come rushing forward. These aircraft use lighter and more aerodynamic airframes and more efficient engines. Modern jets also have better compatibility with sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

The sustainability advantages also boost a carrier's profit margins. Using less fuel to fly larger aircraft greater distances reduces costs incurred per seat. Carriers lose less of your airfare to these costs while flying modern aircraft.

Which Legacy Carrier Flies The Oldest Aircraft

The United States' three legacy carriers all have fleets of relatively similar ages. United Airlines has the oldest fleet, with an average aircraft age of 15.3 years. This is followed by Delta Air Lines at 15 years. American Airlines has the youngest fleet with an average age of 14.5 years.

The table below shows the oldest aircraft flown by US legacy carriers, selecting from planespotters.net data on American, United, and Delta on aircraft types over 20 years. It includes the plane's average age and the total in each carrier's fleet:

The average age trend is mirrored by the number of aircraft each carrier has in its fleet, with an average age of over 20 years. The youngest fleet, American, has 244 such aircraft spread across just three families. The Airbus A319 is by far the most prevalent, and old examples of this jet are also present among the other two legacy carriers. The second-oldest fleet, Delta, has five aircraft types averaging over 20 years old with a total of 331 aircraft. The most bizarre within this fleet are the 80 717s. Finally, the oldest fleet, United has 352 jets over 20 years old. These planes are also spread across five aircraft types. The presence of families like the Boeing 757 and 767 is rather predictable.

Why Is There Such Longevity?

The most important reason an aircraft would keep flying is that it remains safe to do so. “Over time, every part of the plane will be replaced with a new part,” InsiJets notes, regarding how proper maintenance can keep an aircraft flying for far longer than expected. “However, older aircraft still have more operational issues, such as faults with heating and plumbing.” Such faults can be tolerated given the astronomical costs of replacing an old aircraft with a modern equivalent. A single Boeing 777X has list prices in excess of $400 million. Many carriers won't be able to make up this cost in operational savings. For that reason, and the fact that most strain on the aircraft happens during takeoff and landing, long-haul widebody aircraft tend to have longer lifespans than short-haul narrowbody jets.

Old aircraft also have usually been completely paid off with no outstanding lease or loan payments. These are also assets with little room for further depreciation. Costs outside of basic operations and maintenance are limited.

Carriers have to undergo hefty challenges to keep jets over 20 years old in the sky. Three types of maintenance checks are needed. A-Check is undergone every 400-800 flight hours, with mechanics checking basic systems. C-Check happens every 20-24 months with more structural checks. Finally, a D-Check is done every 6-10 years and involves a full airframe teardown and rebuild. The latter will keep a jet out of operation for an extended period.

How The COVID-19 Pandemic Increased Aircraft's Lifespans

An aircraft's true age isn't measured by the number of years since it left the factory, but by the number of times it has flown and the distance it has covered. During the COVID-19 pandemic, travel bans were in place, so aircraft spent far longer than usual on the ground. Time in storage was time spent not flying and incurring wear.

Mechanics also took the opportunity to conduct more extensive maintenance than they would usually have time for. Thorough maintenance allowed issues to be spotted before they could become a problem that would force an airframe to be retired. It will be interesting to see if the current conflict in the Middle East will have any similar impacts, given the enormous amount of disruption to the industry already caused:

On the other hand, the pandemic offered an opportunity to retire aircraft. Flight Global reported in 2020 that “the coronavirus travel downturn is accelerating the retirement of aircraft that are older, less fuel-efficient, and higher maintenance.” These retirements occurred because carriers no longer needed to meet capacity demands. The pandemic brought them time to conduct extensive reshuffling of their fleets towards newer jets.

The Delta 717 Case Study

The choice to fly old aircraft is often made because they continue to fulfill a role effectively that modern jets can't account for. Delta Air Lines' Boeing 717s are slightly different because the jet's longevity is due to the carrier's rich history with McDonnell Douglas aircraft. It previously had sizable fleets of the MD-88 and MD-90, with the last of these examples being retired in 2020. Delta handles maintenance through its in-house TechOps team, who have tremendous experience dealing with older McDonnell Douglas aircraft.

Similar experience of McDonnell Douglas aircraft among the carrier's pilots and crew also allows the 717 to continue to operate seamlessly. All this is relevant as the aircraft was first developed in the 1990s by McDonnell Douglas under the name MD-85, becoming the 717 when the manufacturer merged with Boeing in August 1997.

Delta Air Lines currently operates 80 717s with 73 in active service and seven parked for maintenance. It has also had to retire 24 of these aircraft. The planes continue to be used prolifically, with Cirium data revealing 12,648 flights and 1.4 million seats planned in June 2025. The main impact of the 717 has been to remove 2.2 50-seat regional jets from Delta's fleet per 717, giving the carrier a decrease in seat costs and an increase in economy and premium class capacity.

Cargo Carriers And Old Aircraft

Cargo carriers are particularly prevalent operators of old aircraft. FedEx Express's aircraft have an average age of 20.7 years, slightly higher than UPS Airlines' 19.8 years. Meanwhile, DHL Aviation has some jets over 35 years old. Atlas Air has 50% of its fleet nearing 30 years old. Old aircraft are popular amongst cargo carriers as they are cheaper to purchase, often converted from passenger airliners that have reached the end of their life in commercial aviation. That means cargo carriers can turn a quick profit. Issues with higher operating and maintenance costs are less of an issue as cargo jets tend to fly less frequently than passenger airliners.

The nature of cargo flying also puts less of a strain on the aircraft. Cargo jets fly longer routes as short-haul cargo tends to be conducted by truck or train. These planes spend less time conducting takeoffs and landings, flight phases that cause the greatest strain, compared with cruising.

All this isn't to say that cargo carriers only fly outdated aircraft. Some cargo carriers have put in orders for modern jets like the 777X freighter. Yet, this is more a case of dipping their toes into modern flying, while the cheap acquisition costs of older planes continue to win out.

text:
If you have been following business aviation lately, you have probably noticed a clear shift. It is no longer just about the speed, luxury, or flexibility; it is about carbon footprint, sustainability, and accountability.

For private aviation, this shift is no longer optional. It is being driven by regulators, corporate clients, and changing public expectations. Let’s break this down in a structured and easy-to-understand way.

What Is Carbon Footprint in Aviation?

Carbon footprint refers to the total greenhouse gas emissions, mainly carbon dioxide (CO₂), produced by aviation activities. These emissions primarily come from burning jet fuel.

Key Points:

Aviation contributes around 2–2.5% of global CO₂ emissions

Business aviation accounts for 2–4% of total aviation emissions

Per passenger, private jets can emit 5–14 times more CO₂ than commercial flights

What This Means:

Even though private aviation is a smaller segment, its per-passenger impact is significantly higher, making it a focal point in sustainability discussions.

Why Carbon Footprint Matters More Than Ever

1. Changing Public Perception

The conversation around climate change has made private aviation more visible.

Impact:

Increased media and environmental scrutiny

Growing pressure on high-emission travel

Demand for transparency

2. Corporate ESG Commitments

Many companies now follow Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) frameworks. Business aviation providers are now expected to align with corporate sustainability goals.

What Companies Are Doing:

Tracking travel-related emissions

Choosing sustainable operators

Investing in carbon offset programs

3. Operational Efficiency Is Now Environmental

Efficiency directly affects emissions. Even small inefficiencies can significantly increase fuel burn and emissions.

Factors Increasing Carbon Output:

Longer routes due to geopolitical conflicts

Airspace closures

Holding patterns and delays

Empty leg flights

What Contributes to a Private Jet’s Carbon Footprint?

Understanding the components helps identify where improvements can be made.

1. Fuel Burn

Fuel burn remains the single largest contributor to aviation emissions, making it the most critical factor in understanding environmental impact. Every flight’s carbon footprint is directly tied to how much fuel is consumed, which in turn depends on the aircraft type, route, and total flight duration. Longer flights and less fuel-efficient aircraft naturally produce higher emissions, making fuel optimization a key focus area for operators aiming to reduce their environmental footprint.

2. Non-CO₂ Effects

While carbon dioxide often dominates sustainability discussions, aviation’s environmental impact extends far beyond CO₂ emissions. Aircraft also release nitrogen oxides (NOx), create contrails, and emit particulate matter at high altitudes. These non-CO₂ effects can significantly amplify overall climate impact by influencing atmospheric chemistry and cloud formation, sometimes making the total impact of a flight much greater than what CO₂ emissions alone would suggest.

3. Aircraft Type and Passenger Load

The type of aircraft and how it is utilized play a crucial role in determining emissions per passenger. Larger jets typically consume more fuel overall, but their efficiency improves when more passengers are onboard. Conversely, flights with fewer passengers result in higher emissions per person, which is often a concern in private aviation. Optimizing aircraft size and improving load factors can therefore make a meaningful difference in reducing per-passenger emissions.

4. Flight Distance and Profile

Flight distance and operational profile also significantly influence fuel efficiency. Short-haul flights tend to be less efficient because a large portion of fuel is consumed during the takeoff and climb phases—both of which are the most energy-intensive parts of a flight. As a result, shorter journeys can have disproportionately high emissions relative to distance traveled, highlighting the importance of route planning and operational efficiency in minimizing environmental impact.

Key Regulations Shaping Business Aviation

Regulations are the biggest drivers of change in this space.

1. EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS)

The EU Emissions Trading System is one of the most established mechanisms designed to control aviation emissions by putting a direct price on carbon. Under this system, operators are required to purchase carbon credits for the emissions they produce, while an overall cap on emissions is gradually reduced over time. In addition, free allowances that were once widely available are steadily being phased out, increasing the financial pressure on operators.

For business aviation, this translates into higher operational costs and a growing need to actively manage emissions. At the same time, it creates a strong incentive to adopt more efficient practices and explore sustainable alternatives such as cleaner fuels.

2. CORSIA (Global Offset Scheme)

The CORSIA, introduced by the International Civil Aviation Organization, represents a global effort to stabilize emissions from international aviation. Instead of directly limiting emissions, CORSIA requires airlines to offset their growth in emissions by investing in certified environmental projects. This scheme applies specifically to international flights and has been widely adopted by countries around the world.

For business aviation, it marks a shift toward standardized carbon offset programs and greater accountability, making emissions tracking and reporting an essential part of operations.

3. ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation

The ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation is one of the most impactful recent policies aimed at accelerating the use of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF). It mandates that fuel suppliers gradually blend SAF into conventional jet fuel, starting with 2% by 2025 and increasing significantly to 70% by 2050. This regulation forces a structural shift in how aviation fuel is sourced and used.

In the short term, operators may face higher fuel costs due to the limited availability and higher price of SAF. However, in the long run, it lays the foundation for a more sustainable aviation ecosystem and reduces dependence on traditional fossil fuels.

4. Net-Zero by 2050 Target

The global aviation sector has aligned itself with the ambitious goal of achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, a target supported by organizations like the International Air Transport Association. Reaching this goal will require a multi-faceted approach, including the widespread adoption of sustainable aviation fuels, the development of advanced aircraft technologies, and significant improvements in operational efficiency.

Carbon offsetting will also play a supporting role in balancing residual emissions. For business aviation, this commitment signals a long-term transformation, where sustainability will no longer be optional but a core part of strategy and operations.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel is a Core Solution

Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is emerging as a central pillar in aviation’s strategy to reduce carbon emissions and transition toward a more sustainable future. As the industry faces increasing regulatory pressure and environmental scrutiny, SAF offers a practical and scalable solution that can be used with existing aircraft and infrastructure. Unlike long-term innovations such as electric or hydrogen-powered aircraft, SAF can be implemented immediately, making it a critical tool in achieving near-term emission reduction targets.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel is a cleaner alternative to conventional jet fuel, designed to significantly lower lifecycle carbon emissions. It is produced from a variety of non-fossil-based sources, including waste oils, agricultural residues, and synthetic processes that capture carbon from the atmosphere. These feedstocks are processed into fuel that meets the same safety and performance standards as traditional aviation fuel, allowing it to be blended and used without requiring modifications to aircraft engines. By utilizing renewable and waste-based inputs, SAF helps reduce dependence on fossil fuels while supporting a circular economy approach to energy production

Benefits of SAF

Sustainable Aviation Fuel can reduce lifecycle emissions by up to 80% by using renewable or waste-based feedstocks, significantly lowering the overall carbon footprint compared to conventional fossil-based jet fuel.

SAF is designed as a “drop-in” fuel, meaning it can be blended with traditional jet fuel and used in current aircraft engines without requiring modifications, ensuring easy and cost-effective adoption for operators.

Since SAF works within existing aviation infrastructure, it enables operators to reduce emissions immediately without waiting for new technologies, aircraft designs, or major investments in fueling and distribution systems.

Challenges of SAF

Sustainable Aviation Fuel is currently produced in very limited quantities, making it difficult for widespread adoption. Supply constraints prevent airlines and operators from fully transitioning despite growing demand and regulatory pressure.

SAF remains significantly more expensive than conventional jet fuel due to complex production processes, limited scale, and feedstock costs, increasing operational expenses, and making affordability a major challenge for widespread use.

The expansion of SAF production is progressing slowly due to technological, financial, and infrastructure barriers, limiting the pace at which supply can meet global aviation demand and slowing overall industry decarbonization efforts.

Currently, SAF accounts for less than 1% of total aviation fuel use.

How Carbon Footprint Is Transforming Business Aviation

Carbon footprint is becoming an important factor in business aviation and is changing how the industry works. Earlier, it was not a major concern, but now companies and travelers are paying more attention to how flights impact the environment. This shift is pushing the industry toward more responsible and sustainable practices.

Regulations: Rules Are Getting Stricter

Governments and aviation authorities are introducing new rules to control emissions. These rules require operators to track, report, and reduce their carbon output. Because of this, companies are now focusing more on cleaner operations and following environmental standards more seriously.

Operations: Costs Are Rising, Efficiency Matters

As sustainability becomes important, costs are increasing due to cleaner fuels, carbon programs, and compliance requirements. To manage this, operators are improving efficiency by better planning flights, reducing empty trips, and using shared flying options wherever possible.

Technology: Moving Toward Cleaner Aircraft

Customer Expectations: Travelers Are More Aware

A Defining Shift for Business Aviation

The carbon footprint conversation is no longer theoretical—it is actively reshaping business aviation.

Key Takeaways:

Sustainability is now a core industry driver

Regulations are accelerating change

Costs and operations are evolving

Customer expectations are shifting

The future of business aviation lies in balancing performance, efficiency, and environmental responsibility. In simple terms, the question is no longer: “Can private aviation become sustainable?” It is: “How fast can it adapt?”

text:
2026年3月27日、JFEエンジニアリング㈱は、国立大学法人富山大学と共同で、航空分野の脱炭素化において最も期待されている手段である持続可能な航空燃料（Sustainable Aviation Fuel: SAF）を製造可能な新触媒を開発したと発表した。

この新触媒は、一酸化炭素（CO）と水素（H2）の混合ガスからSAFを製造するために必要なFischer-Tropsch（FT)合成に用いられるものであり、富山大学学術研究部工学系の椿範立教授が開発した触媒の性能を高め、SAFに適した液体炭化水素の収率が50%以上となる高い性能を持つことから、生産性の高いSAF合成プロセスが実現できる。

従来のFT合成触媒では、得られる炭化水素を水素化分解によりSAFに適した炭素数に変換することが必要となり、この水素化分解でのロスも含めるとSAFの収率は25％程度に留まる。一方、今回新たに開発した触媒を使用したFT合成は、多額の設備投資が必要な水素化分解プラントと水素の新規投入が不要になるため設備コストが大幅に削減できるだけでなく、FT合成のみのプロセスでSAFを従来比2倍以上の収率で製造することができる。

現状国内外のSAF製造の原料は廃食油が中心であるが、食用油資源の供給不足の観点からバイオマスや都市ごみなどの廃棄物へ多様化していき、長期的には発電所や工場から排出され回収したCO2と再エネ由来などの水素（H2）を合成して製造される合成燃料が重要な位置づけを占めると予想されている。これらの原料からSAFを製造するには、FT合成が不可欠であり、そのFT合成に今回の新触媒が活かされることになる。

JFEエンジニアリングと富山大学は、本触媒によるSAF合成プロセスのさらなる開発を継続するとともに、SAFの普及拡大を通じて航空分野の脱炭素化の実現に貢献していく考えだ。

詳しくは、→https://www.jfe-eng.co.jp/news/2026/20260327.html

3h

Singapore has postponed the rollout of its sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) levy, delaying a plan that would have added a new charge to tickets sold for departing flights later in 2026.

The Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) announced on 25 March 2026 that the levy will now apply to tickets and services sold from 1 October 2026 for flights departing from 1 January 2027. Under the previous timetable, it was due to apply to tickets sold from 1 April 2026 for flights departing from 1 October 2026.

CAAS said the delay was made because of the impact of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East on airlines and passengers. The authority also stressed that Singapore remains committed to aviation decarbonisation, but is taking what it described as a pragmatic pause while monitoring global developments.

The SAF levy is intended to help fund the use of cleaner aviation fuel on flights departing Singapore. Passenger charges are expected to vary by route and cabin class, with previously announced figures ranging from S$1 to S$41.60.

Singapore has also adjusted its near-term sustainability timeline, with its 1% SAF target for departing flights now applying from 2027 instead of 2026, while the longer-term ambition of 3% to 5% by 2030 remains in place, subject to global developments and fuel availability.

title: Cum pot fermierii români să contribuie la economia industriilor sustenabile prin culturi intermediare
description:
Fermierii români cultivă deja suprafețe extinse cu plante oleaginoase și se află printre principalii producători de floarea-soarelui din Uniunea Europeană.
Dincolo de piețele tradiționale de hrană și furaje, aceste culturi pot furniza și materii prime pentru combustibili sustenabili pentru aviație, produși în conformitate cu standardele europene stricte.
Inovația tehnologică și colaborarea în lanțul valoric Inovația tehnologică va fi esențială pentru extinderea eficientă a sistemelor de culturi secundare.
Această definiție are un impact direct asupra deciziilor de plantare și a planificării investițiilor la nivelul fermelor.
Fără reguli clare și flexibile, producătorii pot ezita să adopte sistemele de culturi intermediare din cauza incertitudinii privind eligibilitatea pe piață.
text:
Drumul Europei către neutralitatea climatică transformă profund sectoarele care se confruntă cu provocări majore de decarbonizare, iar aviația se numără printre cele mai afectate.

Întrucât aeronavele nu pot fi electrificate, iar tehnologiile alternative de propulsie sunt încă insuficient dezvoltate, combustibilul sustenabil pentru aviație (Sustainable Aviation Fuel – SAF) reprezintă, în prezent, cea mai viabilă soluție pentru reducerea emisiilor din transportul aerian.

Reglementările europene impun deja introducerea SAF în amestec, pornind de la 2% și crescând progresiv până la 70% până în anul 2050, ceea ce transformă piața combustibililor pentru aviație și generează o cerere semnificativă pentru materii prime sustenabile, produse la scară largă.

În acest context, decarbonizarea aviației nu mai este doar o problemă industrială și de mediu, ci și una agricolă, deoarece leagă politicile energetice de economiile rurale și de deciziile de producție la nivelul fermelor din întreaga Uniune Europeană.

Rolul României și potențialul agricol

În acest cadru european mai larg, țările cu baze agricole solide sunt în mod natural bine poziționate pentru a juca un rol important, iar România este un exemplu relevant.

Agricultura rămâne un contributor strategic la PIB și la ocuparea forței de muncă în mediul rural, iar dezvoltarea biocombustibililor avansați oferă fermierilor o cale practică de diversificare și creare de valoare.

Fermierii români cultivă deja suprafețe extinse cu plante oleaginoase și se află printre principalii producători de floarea-soarelui din Uniunea Europeană.

Dincolo de piețele tradiționale de hrană și furaje, aceste culturi pot furniza și materii prime pentru combustibili sustenabili pentru aviație, produși în conformitate cu standardele europene stricte.

Culturile intermediare ca sursă de valoare economică

O oportunitate majoră constă în extinderea culturilor intermediare sau secundare cultivate între ciclurile agricole principale: soiurile oleaginoase cu ciclu scurt pot fi recoltate și valorificate comercial, transformând practicile de conservare a solului în surse suplimentare de venit.

Fermierii adoptă treptat aceste sisteme, prin semănarea culturilor oleaginoase după grâu și integrarea rotațiilor cu plante precum floarea-soarelui, crescând productivitatea terenurilor fără extinderea suprafețelor agricole sau competiție cu producția alimentară.

Acest potențial este susținut și de politicile naționale care vizează atingerea unui prag de 1% biocombustibili avansați până în 2025 și 3,5% până în 2030, în timp ce baza agricolă solidă a României, fermele comerciale și infrastructura existentă creează condiții favorabile pentru creșterea producției și furnizarea de materii prime către piața emergentă a combustibililor sustenabili pentru aviație.

Inovația tehnologică și colaborarea în lanțul valoric

Inovația tehnologică va fi esențială pentru extinderea eficientă a sistemelor de culturi secundare. Companii precum Corteva Agriscience, companie internațională de știință și tehnologie agricolă, investesc peste 4 milioane de dolari zilnic în cercetare și dezvoltare și operează mai mult de 120 de centre R&D la nivel global, oferind fermierilor soluții agricole avansate.

Acestea includ hibrizi oleaginoși de înaltă performanță, cu producții îmbunătățite, cicluri de vegetație mai scurte și o reziliență sporită la stresul climatic — caracteristici-cheie pentru integrarea culturilor intermediare, menținând în același timp sănătatea și productivitatea solului pe termen lung. În paralel, colaborarea de-a lungul întregului lanț valoric contribuie la conectarea producției agricole cu cererea din sectorul energiei regenerabile.

De exemplu, Etlas, societatea mixtă dintre Corteva Agriscience și bp, demonstrează cum inovația poate reuni expertiza în genetică vegetală cu capacitățile din sectorul energetic, creând un flux mai predictibil de materii prime agricole pentru combustibili sustenabili pentru aviație și motorină regenerabilă, oferind totodată fermierilor noi oportunități de venit.

Importanța cadrului de reglementare european

La nivel european, predictibilitatea reglementărilor este la fel de importantă. Comisia Europeană definește în prezent termenul de „cultură intermediară” în cadrul legislației privind energia regenerabilă, clasificare care va determina ce produse agricole sunt eligibile pentru piețele biocombustibililor.

Această definiție are un impact direct asupra deciziilor de plantare și a planificării investițiilor la nivelul fermelor.

Fără reguli clare și flexibile, producătorii pot ezita să adopte sistemele de culturi intermediare din cauza incertitudinii privind eligibilitatea pe piață. Un cadru de reglementare stabil ar oferi fermierilor încrederea necesară pentru a-și diversifica producția, aliniindu-se în același timp obiectivelor de decarbonizare ale Europei.

Oportunitatea pentru fermierii români

Cu politici favorabile, inovație tehnologică continuă și o coordonare mai strânsă între sectoarele agricol și energetic, fermierii români sunt bine poziționați pentru a deveni furnizori de încredere în lanțul valoric al combustibililor sustenabili pentru aviație, consolidând în același timp competitivitatea pe termen lung a economiei rurale.

Autor: Sergii Kharin, Country Leader la Corteva Agriscience în România și Republica Moldova

Despre Corteva Agriscience

Corteva Agriscience este o companie globală, eminamente agricolă, tranzacționată la bursă, ce combină inovația de vârf din industrie, implicarea clienților și execuția operațională pentru a oferi soluții la cele mai mari provocări agricole din lume.

Corteva generează opțiuni avantajoase pe piață prin strategia sa unică de distribuție, împreună cu mixul său echilibrat și divers de semințe, produse de protecția a plantelor și servicii digitale la nivel mondial.

Având în portofoliu unele dintre cele mai cunoscute mărci din agricultură și o linie de produse și tehnologii de top în industrie, ce pot genera creșteri viitoare, compania se angajează să maximizeze productivitatea fermierilor, colaborand in acelasi timp cu părțile interesate din întreg sistemul alimentar, contribuind la promisiunea de a îmbogăți viața celor care produc și a celor care consumă și asigurând progresul generațiilor viitoare.
